question: Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the resulting sanctions, European businesses have turned to the Trans-Caspian international transport route (TITR) to ship goods to Central Asia. However, they are encountering infrastructure challenges and increased costs.

This situation is threatening European companies’ presence in Central-Asian markets, where they are potentially losing ground to Chinese and Russian competitors. Without EU intervention, there is a risk of their withdrawing from these markets.

Safeguarding the EU’s strategic economic interests in third countries is paramount, encompassing support for key industries, exporting modern technologies and implementing the Critical Raw Materials Act1. Despite these efforts, the competitiveness of EU businesses exporting to the region will continue to be impacted until significant improvements are made in the TITR.
This situation prompts several critical questions. 1.
What projects does the Commission intend to launch to support the EU industry competitiveness with the announced funding?
What additional funding opportunities and support does the Commission plan to offer to European businesses in this regard?
Will the Commission fast track this support, so that it arrives on time for companies that are struggling to maintain their presence in Central-Asian markets?
Proposal for a Regulation establishing a framework for ensuring a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials (COM(2023)0160).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2024) The EU provides international cooperation funding in Central Asia, in line with the 2019 EU-Central Asia Strategy1, including transport cooperation. Through its European Fund for Sustainable Development Plus (EFSD+)2 blending facilities, it also uses grants and loans for non-bankable investment projects in partner countries.

The use of EFSD+ guarantees allows investors to finance projects in challenging markets. Loan beneficiaries can be private companies, but EU projects do not directly fund companies, except when contracting services or goods for project implementation.

In the framework of the Global Gateway strategy3, the Commission expects that its ongoing work on improving transparency, prioritisation, and coordination of the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor (TCTC) will also create opportunities for interested EU companies to invest in projects in Central Asia.

As announced at the Investors’ Forum in January 2024, the EU and its partners will commit, overall, EUR 10 billion to invest in sustainable transport connectivity in Central Asia4. Another key deliverable of the Forum was the EU’s announcement to establish a Coordination Platform5, to enhance cooperation and ensure that development of the TCTC stays on track.
The Commission’s competitiveness agenda6 focusses on the ability of businesses to be productive and to grow while avoiding supply chain disruptions.

The EU has negotiated (with Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan) and is negotiating (with Tajikistan) enhanced Partnership and Cooperation Agreements, which contain extensive provisions on public procurement, investment in trade and services, state owned enterprises, etc. The Agreements are in force with Kazakhstan7 and expected to be signed with Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan later in 2024.

The Commission has also signed Memorandums of Understanding on Critical Raw Materials with Kazakhstan8 and Uzbekistan9 to strengthen cooperation in raw materials, particularly through identifying joint investments and supporting their development. 1 https://www.eeas.europa.eu/eeas/basis-eu-%E2%80%93-central-asia-cooperation_en 2 https://international-partnerships.ec.europa.
